newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parties at deadlock over new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parties at deadlock over new cabinet.

text.p: President Petar Stoyanov mediated a new round of talks between Bulgaria's rival political factions on Friday but the two sides remained as far apart as ever on forming a new cabinet.
The opposition plans an 18th consecutive day of rallies later on Friday against the ex-communist Socialists' plans to form a new cabinet, and for a quick general election.

The constitution requires Stoyanov, who took office on Wednesday, to ask the Socialists as the biggest party in parliament to form a new government, but the opposition has threatened mass protests and a general strike if he does so.
Leaders of the two parliamentary groups met together at the presidency for more than two hours but showed no sign of compromise.
Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said he saw no point in more talks.
"Unfortunately, there is a complete difference between the positions and assessments of the United Democratic Forces and the Democratic Left," he said, referring to the two parliamentary coalitions.
"We concluded that dialogue did not take place. I see no need for further talks which could mislead public opinion that compromise is possible."

Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov, attempting a more positive interpretation, said they had agreed on the need for economic reforms and for measures to ease social tension, but his party still insisted on forming a cabinet.

"We suggested a cabinet of experts with broad support from society. From this point on, although they (the opposition) are not prepared enough for talks, dialogue may and should continue to clarify the nature of the tasks, the programme and the laws that should be passed," Parvanov said.

Stoyanov told reporters he had warned against any untenable "Balkan compromise" and had said the Socialists' proposal to form a broad-based cabinet of technocrats was unlikely to win popular confidence.
"I asked them to consider the interests of Bulgaria and from this point of view what will happen if they fail," he said.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but until then they want to form a new cabinet to replace that of Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.
Stoyanov, under pressure to break the deadlock before he leaves on Tuesday night for a visit to Brussels, said he would give the mandate "in a reasonable term".
"I have opened the door, the exact date is not important, much more important is what will happen afterwards," he said.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government failed to implement the last reform programme.

In the meantime, the national currency is in freefall. The lev traded at new lows of 910-915 on the interbank market on Friday on expectations on further political instability and the knowledge that the central bank lacks the funds to support it.
The Socialist-dominated parliament appointed 11 new judges to the Supreme Court on Friday in the absence of the UDF, which is boycotting the assembly until it approves a quick election.

The Supreme Court, previously dominated by UDF nominees, has supported the president's veto on certain laws in the past. The court operates as a last resort if parliament overrules a presidential veto.
Nine of the new judges were proposed by the Socialists, one by the small Bulgarian Business Bloc, and one by the ethnic Turkish UDF-allied Movement for Rights and Freedoms.
